title: The Content Factory
subtitle: Brands built a factory to make their goods and a warehouse to store them. Now they need both again, for content.

content.text: A few nights ago I was going back through a pitch we had made for an innerwear brand. It is a good brand: premium, with very particular founders and a catalogue that honestly looks fantastic. Somewhere around page twenty I realised the whole pitch was wrong.

We had walked in to sell them catalogue possibilities: better backgrounds, new models, new poses, macros of the yarn, all of it nicely made. But their catalogue was never the problem. Founders who care that much about every shot do not need someone from outside telling them their shoots could be better.

What they did not have was volume. They had one great reel that did 3.4 million views, and then a long tail of posts that did fine. They had one celebrity they had paid for, and had used him a handful of times. And they had one product page that every person on the internet lands on, whether that person is a 19 year old in Pune or a 52 year old dad buying a three-pack for the drawer.
So the question changed. It stopped being "how do we make your pictures better?" and became "how do we help you make a hundred times more of what already works, without it turning into garbage?"
That question is what this piece is about. I think it is the most important question every consumer brand will face over the next five years, and I think the answer has a very old shape.
The Two Buildings
Every product brand on earth runs on two buildings.
There is a
factory
, where the goods get made, and a
warehouse
, where the goods get stored, counted, labelled and sent out. Then there is a shop, a website or a marketplace, where somebody buys them.

Nobody thinks this is clever; it is simply how things work. But it is worth remembering that it wasn't always this way. Before the factory, goods were made by hand, one at a time, by craftsmen who carried the knowledge of how to make them in their heads. The great leap of the industrial era was not just machines; it was turning that tacit knowledge into a process that anyone could run. When Ford introduced the moving assembly line at Highland Park in 1913, the breakthrough was as much about writing the work down, breaking it into stations with a defined order, as it was about the conveyor belt.

You would never run a clothing brand today where every t-shirt was made by hand, from scratch, by a different person each time, with no record of what the last t-shirt looked like. Each shirt would cost a fortune, they would all look slightly different, and you could never make enough of them.
That, however, is exactly how almost every brand makes content today.

Every shoot starts from zero. A brief gets written, a photographer gets booked, models get cast, a location gets found, a day gets spent, the files go to an editor, the editor sends them to the brand, the brand sends notes, and three weeks later you have forty usable images. Then the next campaign starts from zero again. The knowledge of what worked last time lives in a few people's heads and a few Google Drive folders with names like "FINAL_final_v3".
Content, in other words, is still a craft industry. It is beautiful sometimes, but it is handmade, and handmade does not scale.
Now Add a Second Line
This is the whole idea in one picture:
Brands are going to run a second line, directly under the first one. The shape is the same; the material is different.
An
AI warehouse
, where you store everything that makes your brand your brand. Not the goods: the context.
A
content factory
, built around that warehouse, which turns that context into reels, pages, product pages, films and ads, every day, at a volume no team of humans could ever shoot.
You make clothes in a factory and keep them in a warehouse. Now you keep your brand in a warehouse and make your content in a factory.
That is the pitch I should have made to that innerwear brand from the start. Everything below is about how it actually works, why it is suddenly possible, and why it does not have to turn into slop.
What Lives in the Warehouse

When people hear "AI warehouse" they think of a folder of logos and a brand guidelines PDF. That is maybe five percent of it. A real warehouse holds every piece of context that a great creative director carries around in their head, written down so that a machine can use it. In practice, that is about nine shelves.
1. Every SKU, captured properly.

Front, back, side, flat, folded, on a body and in macro. The real colour under daylight, not the colour your monitor thinks it is. The rib of the waistband; how the fabric drapes and how it creases. This is the shelf people underestimate. If the model does not know exactly what your product is, everything downstream drifts, and the first person to notice is your customer.
2. Fabric and macros.
The yarn, the weave, the stitch, the label. For apparel, and for a lot of consumer goods, this is where trust lives. People zoom in.
3. The real faces.

Models you have actually shot, with consent, captured as character sheets: the same person from many angles and in many lights, with real skin and pores. And, importantly, a rule: you never generate a likeness you do not have the rights to. If you have a celebrity, you work from footage you own. You do not fake a face.
4. Reviews, word for word.

What customers actually say. "Waistband doesn't roll." "Survived 100 washes." "Bought it for my dad, he wears nothing else now." This is the best copy you will ever have, and most brands leave it sitting in a reviews widget.
5. Winners.
Every post, reel and ad that worked, with the numbers: what the hook was, how long it held attention, which product, which placement.
6. Brand voice.
How you talk, and how you never talk.
7. Fonts, colours, logo and layouts.
The boring stuff, which is precisely the stuff that makes content look like it came from you.
8. Rules.
"Never show the product on a white seamless." "Never put text straight on a busy photo." "Never shoot him smiling with teeth." Every brand has thirty of these, and they are almost never written down.
9. What got rejected.
This is the shelf nobody builds, and it may be the most valuable one. Every time a human looks at an output and says no, that no is information. Store it.

Technically, this is not one database; it is a few things stitched together. Images and videos sit in an asset store with tags. Products become what we call product twins: a set of reference images plus a structured description (colour codes, fabric, construction, fit) that gets passed into every generation. Text like reviews, rules and voice gets embedded, so that a brief can pull the ten most relevant pieces of context for that particular job. Performance data comes in from the ad platforms and Instagram. And rejections are logged against the prompt and the model that produced them, so the system learns what this particular brand hates.
The key property of a warehouse is that it
gets fuller every day
. Every shoot, every review, every ad that wins or loses goes back on a shelf. Six months in, your warehouse knows more about what works for your brand than any single person in your company does.
How the Factory Runs
The factory is a loop, and the loop has five stations.
Brief.

Somebody, a human or an agent, writes what is needed: "Forty hooks for the new seamless trunk, for men aged 25 to 34, for Reels, using the 'survived 100 washes' review." The factory goes to the warehouse and pulls the product twin, the right faces, the right reviews, the brand rules, and the last five winners that look like this brief.
Make ×100.

This is where the models do the work, and it is not one model; it is a router. Product shots go to one image model because it holds fabric detail best. Lifestyle goes to another because it renders real skin better. Video goes to a third because it handles motion and sound. Copy goes to a language model that has read every review you have ever received. Then everything is resized automatically into every placement: 9:16 for stories, 4:5 for feed, 1:1, 16:9, 1.91:1. One idea, every placement.
Humans pick.
I will come back to this, because it is the whole game. A person, ideally someone with real taste, looks at the hundred and picks three. They say no a lot, and each no goes on the rejected shelf.
Ship.
The three go out: into ads, into organic, onto the product page, into email.
Measure.
The numbers come back: what held attention, what got clicked, what sold, what got comments like "link?".
And then the important part:
what won goes back into the warehouse, and what lost goes back in too.
The loop closes, and the next brief starts smarter than this one did.

This is the difference between a content factory and someone "using AI", which usually means one person typing prompts into a box. A factory has stations, it has memory, and it gets better every time it runs. It is the same leap the assembly line made over the craftsman: not a better tool, but a written-down process that compounds.
Why Now: The Falling Price of a Second of Video

Two years ago, none of this would have made economic sense for video. Images were already getting cheap, but video was slow, short, silent and expensive. That changed quickly this year, and it changed again this week.

On 24 November 2026, Sand.ai released MAGI-2. The numbers are worth sitting with. It is a 480 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model, with roughly 28 billion parameters active at a time. It makes up to 30 seconds of 1080p video at 25 frames a second, with sound, in one pass. It takes up to twenty references: ten images, five videos and five audio clips. And it costs about $0.08 per second of output, which is $2.40 for a 30 second, full HD clip with audio.

For context, Seedance 2.5 at 1080p works out to roughly $0.57 a second, or about $17 for the same 30 seconds. Google's Veo 3.1 lists at about $0.40 a second at 1080p, and Sora 2 Pro sits around $0.70. In one release, the price of a long, finished-looking clip dropped to somewhere between a fifth and a seventh of what the top models charged a few weeks earlier.

Now compare that to the old way. Industry figures for a proper studio day run anywhere from $15,000 to $40,000. A half-day fashion shoot with a model and a photographer is $500 to $2,000 before retouching. A video shoot costs three to ten times what a photo shoot does, and per usable image people quote $300 to $500.

I want to be honest about the limits. These models are not perfect. This week we tried to make a 30 second continuous take on MAGI-2, a man walking through six different eras in one shaky shot, and it timed out three times. Long takes are still hard, so we split it into two 10 second takes and stitched them together. That is exactly the point, though: the tools fail in specific, workable ways, and a factory is built to route around failures. A one-off creator gives up. A factory reroutes.

The direction is not in doubt. A second of good video has gone from a day of a crew's time to less than ten cents. Calling that a 20% saving misses what has happened; it changes what kind of thing content is.
The real unlock is that
trying an idea

gets cheap. When an idea costs three weeks and a lakh of rupees, you try four a month, and you play it safe. When an idea costs an afternoon and a few dollars, you can try four hundred. You can be weird. You can test a hundred times more, keep only what holds up, and pour fuel on that.

This is, I would note, the same pattern Ben Thompson has described for the internet itself: when distribution became free, the scarce thing moved somewhere else. When making content becomes nearly free, the scarce thing stops being the making.
Making Content Almost Free
At ShopOS, this is the thing we wake up thinking about. If the factory is the future, the cost per output has to keep falling until content is close to free for the brand. A few things get us there.
Memory makes it cheaper.

The more a brand uses the warehouse, the fewer generations it takes to get something right. The first time, the model does not know your waistband, so you might need twenty tries. By the hundredth brief, it has your product twin, your rejections and your winners, and it lands in three. Fewer retries is the biggest cost saving there is. Our internal line is simple: the more you use it, the cheaper it gets.
Routing to the cheapest model that is good enough.

Not every job needs the most expensive model. A background swap does not need a 480 billion parameter video model; a hero brand film might. The factory picks the cheapest model that clears the brand's bar for that job, and as new models like MAGI-2 arrive, the router simply starts using them. The brand never has to care.
Reuse.
One shoot day, captured properly into the warehouse, becomes raw material for a year. One licensed celebrity session becomes a thousand cut-downs. You stop paying for the same thing twice.
Credits that work like a utility.
We price generations in credits, so a brand pays for what it makes, not for seats or retainers. As our costs fall, theirs do.

We are also working on things that push the cost even closer to zero, like brands earning credits back when their outputs perform. More on that when it is ready. But the goal is clear: the cost of making content should stop being the reason a brand does not make it.
What a Factory Makes
So you have a warehouse and a factory. What comes out? There are four outputs I think will matter most for a direct-to-consumer brand.
One celebrity, a thousand takes
Most brands that pay for a celebrity get maybe ten pieces of content out of it: a TV spot, a couple of reels, some stills. Then the contract sits there.

With a factory, you take the footage you already own, every second of it, including the moments between takes, and cut it a thousand ways. Different hooks in the first two seconds. Different lengths: 6, 15 and 30 seconds. Different languages and subtitles. Different products cut in. Different placements. Different audiences, so the version for a college student opens with the joke and the version for a dad opens with the comfort line. The celebrity shot for one day; you get a year of content.
There is one rule I will not bend on: you work from footage you have the rights to. You never generate a fake face. The factory is for multiplying what is real, not inventing what is not.
Trust pages

This is something big brands quietly do that small brands should copy. Instead of only posting from the brand account, you run a set of neutral Instagram pages that build trust around the category, without your logo on them.

For an innerwear brand, that might be a page that only does macro shots of fabrics and washing tests; a page that literally washes things a hundred times and shows you what happens; a page of gift ideas for dads; a Gen Z page that is mostly memes about comfort. Fifty of them, each with its own look.

Nobody follows a brand account to be sold to, but people do follow a page that answers a question they actually have. When those pages recommend a product, they carry a kind of trust that a brand post can't buy. Fifty pages, each posting daily, each with its own visual language: no team could shoot that. A factory can make it, because the warehouse already holds every fabric, every macro and every review.

(One caveat worth stating plainly: pages like this need to be honest about who is behind them where the law and the platforms require it. The point is to be genuinely useful about the category, not to fake independence.)
A different product page for everyone
Today, every visitor lands on the same product page. The 19 year old and the 52 year old see the same hero image, the same copy and the same reviews.

In a content factory world, the product page is generated. Someone who arrived from the dads' gift page lands on a page with the box set, a gift message and reviews from people who bought it for their father. Someone who arrived from the fabric page lands on a page that opens with the macro and the wash test. Someone who came from a meme lands on a poster-style page that says "GOOD LUCK CHOOSING ONE" over a rack of eight colours. Same product, same price, same checkout; a different story on the way in.
This only works if you can make those variants cheaply and keep them on-brand, which is exactly what the warehouse is for.
The weird new funnel

Put those together and you get a funnel that looks nothing like the old one. The old funnel was an ad, a product page and a cart: one ad, one page. The new one is a reel, or one of a thousand cut-downs, that sends someone to a trust page matching what they care about. The trust page sends them to a product page made for that kind of person, and that page sends them to the cart. Every step is generated, every step is tested, and every winner goes back into the warehouse.

And you can get properly weird: whimsical brand films drawn as pencil storyboards before anyone spends a rupee; ads that are unhinged on purpose, like a CSI investigation into a missing waistband, a nani reviewing your underwear, or uncles sucking in their bellies at a wedding while one man in shapewear stands there relaxed. These are things a brand would never risk a shoot day on, because a shoot day costs too much to gamble. When an idea costs an afternoon, you can afford to find out.

This obviously works for fashion, but it is the same shape for consumer goods, beauty, food, home, or any brand that grew up on Instagram. Every one of them has products, reviews, faces and winners, and every one of them needs more content than it can shoot.
A Content Factory Need Not Be a Slop Factory
Now the obvious worry. If content gets this cheap, won't the internet simply fill up with garbage?

Yes. Partly, it already has. Scroll for two minutes and you will see it: plastic skin, six fingers, a yellow tint, the same glowing sunset on every post, product shots where the logo melts into the fabric. Slop.
But slop is not what happens when you make a lot of content. Slop is what happens when you make a lot of content
with no memory and no taste.

A slop factory goes from prompt to post. It remembers nothing. No human ever says no. It looks like everyone else, because it draws from the same average of the internet as everyone else, and it gets cheaper and worse at the same time.

A content factory goes from brief, to a hundred options, to three picks. It remembers everything. A human owns the no. It looks like you, because it draws from your warehouse instead of the average, and it gets cheaper and better at the same time. The models are the same; the results are completely different. The difference is the warehouse and the human.
How taste survives

There is a nice historical rhyme in this. Toyota's production system, which reshaped manufacturing in the second half of the twentieth century, is famous for a principle called jidoka, and its most visible tool is the andon cord: any worker on the line can pull it to stop production when they see a defect. The insight was that quality cannot be inspected in at the end; it has to be built in by giving people on the line the authority to say no.
A content factory needs its own andon cord, and in practice, the way we work with brands looks like a jam.

The human says: make forty. The AI makes forty. The human says: no, warmer, less shiny, his skin looks like plastic, the waistband is the wrong green. The AI makes forty more. The human says: that one, keep it. That is the whole craft. It is not one prompt; it is a conversation, and the human is the one who knows when it is right.
I keep saying this to our team:
the soul of the brand lives in the no.

Any machine can produce a yes. A brand is the sum of all the things it refuses to be. Every time a person with taste rejects an output and says why, they teach the factory what the brand is. Store that, respect that, and never automate it away.
A few rules we follow, which I think every content factory should:
Real over perfect.
Real skin, real pores, a bit of grain, like it was shot on a phone and edited by someone who knows what they're doing. No glow, no fake blur, no oversaturated colour.
Product fidelity is non-negotiable.
If the waistband is wrong, it does not ship. Customers notice before you do.
Never fake a real person.
Licensed footage only.
Humans curate.
Every output that reaches a customer was chosen by a person.
Keep the rejects.
They are training data for taste.
Where the Internet Goes Next
Let me zoom out, because I think there is a bigger story. Put quality on one axis and quantity on the other, and you get four places a brand can live.
The craft shop: good, but little.

This is where most good brands are today, including the one I started this piece with. Beautiful work, slow to make, expensive and rare; every piece is a small event. The problem is that the internet does not reward rare anymore. The feed is a firehose, the algorithm wants daily, and a brand that posts four great things a month gets out-shouted by one that posts forty okay things a week.
The ghost town: little, and not good.
Brands that gave up: a post every few weeks, a stock photo, a sale banner. We will skip this one.
The slop factory: lots, and none of it good.

This is where most AI content sits right now. Infinite volume, zero soul. It works for a while because it is cheap and the algorithm likes volume, but it is a race to the bottom. When everyone can make infinite average content, average content is worth nothing. The slop factory is a trap that looks like a shortcut.
The content factory: lots, and all of it good.
The top right: volume and taste at the same time. Until this year this corner was basically empty, because the only way to get there was to have Nike's budget and a hundred people.

So what happens to the internet over the next three years? The cost of making something has fallen through the floor, so the slop corner fills up first, very fast; it is already filling. Feeds get noisier, everything starts to look the same, and people develop a kind of slop-blindness. They scroll past anything that smells generated.

When that happens, two things become very valuable. The first is taste, because it is the only thing that separates you from the noise. The second is volume, because the feed still eats daily and the algorithm still rewards presence. The craft shops have the first. The slop factories have the second. Almost nobody has both.

There are two paths into the top right. A slop factory can try to learn taste, which I think is very hard; taste is not a feature you bolt on. Or a craft shop can learn volume, by building a warehouse out of everything it already knows and a factory around it. I think this is much easier, because the hard part, the taste, is already there. It just has never been written down.
That is the bet:
the craft shops of today are the content factories of tomorrow,

if they build the warehouse. It is also, not coincidentally, why we are building ShopOS as an AI lab that rolls up creative studios. The studios already have the taste. We give them the warehouse and the factory.

There is a second-order effect I find really interesting. When content becomes almost free, content stops being the scarce thing; attention and trust become scarce instead. The brands that win will be the ones whose content people actually believe, whatever the volume: trust pages that are genuinely useful, real reviews, real faces, licensed footage, and product shots that look exactly like what arrives in the box. The factory is a way to make more. The warehouse is a way to make sure more still feels true.
What to Do on Monday
If you run a direct-to-consumer brand, in fashion, consumer goods or anything else that lives on a feed, this is what I would do on Monday.
Start the warehouse.
Not the factory: the warehouse. Put every SKU in, properly, with macros and real colour. Put your reviews in. Put your winners in, with numbers. Write down your thirty rules. 2.
Pick one thing that already works and make a hundred of it.
Your best reel, your best celebrity moment, your best review. Don't start new; accelerate what is already winning. 3.
Put a person with taste at the "pick three" station.
This is your most important hire. Not a prompt engineer: a curator. 4.
Close the loop.
Make sure what wins and what loses both go back in. 5.
Then get weird.
Once the factory runs, spend some of it on things you would never have risked a shoot day on. Trust pages, generated product pages, unhinged ads. Find out.
And don't throw away your shoots. Your shoots are the raw material. The best content factories will run on top of great shoot teams, not instead of them.
The Next Hundred Years

For a hundred years, brands have had a factory for their goods and a warehouse to store them, and nobody questioned it. For the next hundred, they will have a warehouse for their brand and a factory for their content. The brands that win will be the ones that keep a person in the room who says no.
We are building this at ShopOS. If you run a brand and this sounds like what you need, reply, and let's jam.
